newsitem.title: THAILAND: Amnuay sees Thai rates easing after turmoil ends.
newsitem.headline: Amnuay sees Thai rates easing after turmoil ends.

text.p: Finance Minister Amnuay Viravan said on Thursday that high interest rates in Thailand will ease further once the current financial turmoil ends.

"What happened (attacks on the baht and defence by central bank) will not affect further cuts in interest rates. Further rate cuts will definitely happen as we believe the situation will return to normal in the very near future," he told reporters on his return from a regional bank meeting in Tokyo.

Thailand this week was hit by speculative attacks on the baht after rumours of a devaluation and talk that Amnuay may resign. The stock market sank to a near eight-year low after the baht's slump this week.
"In order to solve the economic ills of the country in the long run, interest rates must come down. Financial institutions and the central bank also share this belief," Amnuay added.

Thai interest rates, which are among the highest in the region and which have been kept high by the central bank to defend the baht from speculative attacks and attract foreign inflows, now range between 12.75-13.00 percent.
Earlier this month, several key financial institutions cut minimum lending rates by 25 basis points in response to signals by the central bank that the time may be right to cut rates.
Amnuay has been a proponent of faster cuts in interest rates to stimulate the slowing Thai economy which is expected to grow by just over five percent this year, the lowest in a decade.
High interest rates have brought on a liquidity crunch in the troubled finance and property sectors and slowed down business activities.
The minister also maintained that Thailand had the resources to defend the baht against any further speculative attacks. "Thailand has the ability to defend the baht forever," he said.
During the latest attacks on the baht, several central banks in the region joined the Bank of Thailand with intervention in the market to prop up the ailing baht.
